title: The Nalanda Pupils Who Dug Wells in an Outcaste Village
dek: In December 1958 a young science teacher took pupils and teachers from a Colombo school to labour in an outcaste village, and a movement grew from it.

story.event: Taking Nalanda College students and teachers to work in the outcaste village of Kanatoluwa
story.summary: In December 1958 A. T. Ariyaratne, a science teacher at Nalanda College in Colombo, took students and teachers to Kanatoluwa, an outcaste village in Kurunegala district, where they worked with villagers on wells, latrines, gardens and the school. Having found little promise of change in Ceylon's parties and agencies, he chose donated labour, or shramadana. Other villages asked for camps, and the Sarvodaya Shramadana Movement grew into Sri Lanka's largest voluntary organisation while he kept teaching until 1972.
paragraphs: In early December 1958 a group of teachers and pupils from Nalanda College, a leading secondary school in Colombo, went to work in Kanatoluwa, a poor village in Kurunegala district. Sarvodaya dates the first camp to 6 December. The village was one that much of Ceylon treated as outcaste. Leading the Nalanda party was A. T. Ariyaratne, 27, who taught science at the school.

He had tried other routes first. As a student he had organised a cooperative for coir spinners after learning that middlemen paid an old woman too little to eat, and someone stabbed him to stop it. Later, according to his 1969 Ramon Magsaysay Award citation, he examined Ceylon's twenty-odd political parties, the government agencies and the religious groups, and found little promise of change. From Vinoba Bhave, Gandhi's leading disciple, he took the warning that a movement without personal sharing would be a delusion. So he began with what he could do himself: he asked colleagues to give their labour, and called the trip "an educational experiment".

Accounts of the camp differ in their details. The 1969 citation says 75 teachers and students went and worked with villagers to sink wells, dig latrine pits, clear home gardens and start a school. The New York Times obituary in 2024 counted 40 students and 12 teachers who spent days digging wells, building latrines and repairing the school; another tribute says they built a road. What the accounts share is pupils from a leading Colombo school labouring beside people their society kept at a distance.

Other villages soon asked for camps of their own, and volunteers began giving weekends and school holidays to needs that villagers named. Ariyaratne called the method shramadana, a call to "share their time, thought and energy". He did not leave his job: his son Vinya later said he kept teaching until 1972 and ran the movement after school and in the holidays. By 1969 the citation counted 75,000 trained young volunteers, and at his death in 2024 Sarvodaya worked in more than 15,000 communities.

quote.text: Do human beings in general attain to well-tempered manhood by a course of idling, or by carefully attending to what will be of use? Which will help a man the more to grow in justice and uprightness, to be up and doing, or to sit with folded hands revolving the ways and means of existence?
quote.source_title: The Memorabilia, tr. Henry Graham Dakyns, Project Gutenberg eBook #1177
quote.connection: Socrates is arguing with a man who thinks his free-born kinswomen too well born to work with their hands. Ariyaratne put the same question to a city school, and answered it by taking its pupils to dig latrines in an outcaste village rather than revolving the ways and means.

reflection: Ariyaratne spent a long time looking before he acted: parties, ministries, religious groups. The looking was not wasted; it told him what he would not wait for. Then he did something small enough to start in a school holiday, with people he already knew.

He also kept his job for fourteen years. Not every serious piece of work needs a dramatic leap. If you are building something beside a full working week and a family, a weekend chosen with care, and then a proper rest, may carry further than a grand plan you never have the hours for.
invitation: Pick one thing you have been studying or planning for a long time. Name the smallest part of it that could be done with your own hands in one afternoon, and write down which afternoon that will be.

research_notes: Participant numbers disagree: the 1969 Magsaysay citation says 75 teachers and students; the New York Times obituary (2024, reprinted by the Boston Globe) and George Bond's 2003 study, as quoted on Wikipedia, say 40 students and 12 teachers; AsiaNews says about forty students. The story gives both main figures with their sources. The work done also differs: wells, latrine pits, home gardens and starting a school (Magsaysay); wells, latrines and repairing the school (NYT); building a road (Tricycle). The story names the work two sources agree on and mentions the road. Location: Sarvodaya and Tricycle call Kanatoluwa remote (it is in Kurunegala district); the NYT calls it 'nearby'; the story names the district only. Spelling varies (Kanatoluwa, Kanatholuwa, Kanatolowa). Birth year: 5 November 1931 (NYT, Sarvodaya, Daily Mirror) against 1932 in Tricycle; the story uses 1931, making him 27 in December 1958. Outcome figures: 75,000 trained volunteers in 1969 (Magsaysay) and more than 15,000 communities by 2024 (Tricycle; the Sunday Times said nearly 15,000 villages in 2001); these describe different dates and are given as such. Credit for the camp: search results point to a 2009 Sunday Observer letter by a participant saying the camp was organised by the Department of Rural Development and Cottage Industries, with D. A. Abeysekera as the pioneer of shramadana camps and Ariyaratne supervising Nalanda's group. That page returns 403 to the verifier and could not be read, so it is not cited, but the story says 'leading the Nalanda party' rather than claiming he organised the whole camp. The 'educational experiment' phrase is as reported by Tricycle and Bond. The coir cooperative and the stabbing come from the Magsaysay biography, not from his own account. The Xenophon passage is Socrates' advice to Aristarchus about free-born women working; it is applied by analogy to caste and manual labour.
